Blind review: fresh-set evaluation of a frozen L20 C1.5 intervention candidate.

Read the attached for facts only; no diagnosis provided. Reconstruct what was measured, then list
the top bugs, misinterpretations, and confounds, plus what observation would resolve each. Separate
observation from inference. Do not assume the framing is complete.

Context: 12 never-executed factual questions about animals (naming/leg-count/property). For each,
a frozen intervention (span-corrected template-attenuation replacement at L20, C=1.5) edits a
spider prompt toward a dog or ant donor prompt. A matched-random control uses an in-span random
direction at the same C. Results (from human adjudication of full 128-token continuations;
repetition_bigram_fraction and generated token count are mechanical):

candidate-C1.5: primary (answer+persistent identity+coherence) 6/12. Per type: legs 4/4 (digit+correct
animal+coherent), naming 2/4 (dog rows clean; both ant rows loop "1. Ant 2. Bee 3. Honeybee" to the
128 cap), property 0/4 (spinneret-dog answers "Yes ... has spinnerets" source-bound; spinneret-ant
fabricates "Yes, ants have spinnerets"; liveyoung-dog "the dog does not give birth to live young"
factually false; liveyoung-ant no-op answers No but identity becomes honey bee).
random-C1.5: primary 1/12 (liveyoung-dog: correct prose but leading '0' token; formatting separate).
C0 identity: swap_log_odds_shift 0.0 on all 12. Capped at 128: candidate 3 cells, random 4 cells.
Per-animal candidate: dog 4/6, ant 2/6. total_applied_norm ratio (random/candidate) 1.17-2.60.
Peak GPU ~13.1 GiB. Model Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B rev 851bf6e8, torch 2.13.0.

Q: (1) Does "candidate 6/12 vs random 1/12" support a direction-specific identity/answer carry, or
is it confounded by the random control's 1.2-2.6x larger total-applied-norm? (2) What is the
biggest single misinterpretation risk in reading these numbers? (3) What one cheap test most
reduces uncertainty?
